```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

How would common ownership of Philadelphia National Bank and Girard Trust
change deposit rates? This example uses the included PNB market and supplied
structural parameters to solve that question. Lower deposit rates harm
depositors: these are **input prices**, paid by banks.

You need basic R and an installed `antitrustBayes` package with compatible
structural dependencies. Follow the
[installation instructions](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes#installation).
This guide needs no CmdStan binary, C++ toolchain or estimated fit. Optional
estimation follows in [Estimate demand and compare merger scenarios](posterior-workflow.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes/blob/main/vignettes/posterior-workflow.Rmd));
the [model reference](supply-and-demand.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes/blob/main/vignettes/supply-and-demand.Rmd)) explains the assumptions.

## Supply a structural state and solve the merger

The packaged `pnb` data describes 39 banks. `prices` are deposit interest rates
in percent; `quantities` are deposits in thousands of dollars. `margins` are
positive price-normalized input markdowns and can exceed one. `group` identifies
the owner of each bank's deposit product.

Choose illustrative Logit price sensitivity `alpha = 1`, outside quantity share
`s0 = .015`, and Bertrand conduct (`supply_model = 1L`). These are assumptions,
not posterior estimates. The small outside share is not an observed data column.

```{r merger}
library(antitrustBayes)
data(pnb)
params <- bayes_params(alpha = 1, s0 = .015, supply_model = 1L)
market <- bayes_market(
  prices = pnb$prices, quantities = pnb$quantities, margins = pnb$margins,
  group = pnb$group, outside_price = 1, market_side = "input",
  insideSize = attr(pnb, "insideSize"), labels = pnb$bank
)
fit <- bayes_specify(params, market)
owner_post <- pnb$group
owner_post[owner_post == attr(pnb, "target")] <- attr(pnb, "acquirer")
merger <- antitrust::counterfactual(ownership = owner_post)
result <- simulate(fit, merger, n_draws = 1L, mc.cores = 1L)
```

`bayes_specify()` creates a supplied-state fit without Stan. Its simulation
uses the supplied parameters and observed market geometry; it does not invent
an estimated quality posterior. The ownership change combines the banks named
by the dataset's acquirer and target attributes.

## Read the merging banks' rates

Use the documented `BayesSim` price matrices to display just those two banks:

```{r rates}
party <- pnb$group %in% c(attr(pnb, "acquirer"), attr(pnb, "target"))
rates <- data.frame(bank = pnb$bank,
  before = as.numeric(result@price_pre[[1]][1, ]),
  after = as.numeric(result@price_post[[1]][1, ]))
rates$proportional_change <- rates$after / rates$before - 1
rates[party, ]
```

Compare `after` with `before` in the same interest-rate units. A proportional
change of `-.01` means a 1% relative reduction: a rate of 2 percent becomes
1.98 percent, a .02 percentage-point fall. It does not mean a one-percentage-point
fall. Effects are conditional on the supplied state, not estimated historical
merger effects.

## Measure the market effect

A market index must account for bank size. `calcPriceDelta()` computes a
Paasche index using postmerger quantities and pre/post rates within the same
structural realization. It returns a proportional change, rather than an equal
average of bank-specific proportional changes.

```{r index}
index <- calcPriceDelta(result, market = TRUE, index = "paasche")
index[c("mean", "n_draws", "n_valid")]
```

In this illustrative state both merging banks lower rates, and the market
index falls about 3.17%. The negative sign means harm to depositors in this
model. Check `n_valid` against `n_draws` before interpretation. Here one supplied
state gives one requested realization; the `mean` is its effect, not a posterior
average with estimated uncertainty. Supplying several illustrative parameter
values would still not turn them into an estimated posterior.

You can stop here with a complete deterministic merger calculation. To learn
about fitting demand, retaining posterior demand states and making paired
scenario comparisons, continue to the optional
[posterior workflow](posterior-workflow.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes/blob/main/vignettes/posterior-workflow.Rmd)). Its inference and evidence steps
are explicitly separate from this lightweight example. `?bayes_specify`,
`?bayes_market` and `?"BayesSim-methods"` describe the public interfaces.
